Q: How to install .sys file into c:\windows\system32\drivers with Inno Setup? A:

By default the {win}\system32 is redirected to {win}\SysWOW64 by the OS for 32-bit applications (like Inno Setup).

You can override this using 64bit flag:

Source: "C:\myproject\driver.sys"; DestDir: "{win}\system32\drivers"; Flags: 64bit

64bit: Causes the {sys} constant to map to the 64-bit System directory when used in the Source and DestDir parameters, .... This is the default behavior in a 64-bit mode install.

Or enable 64-bit mode install.

[Setup]
ArchitecturesInstallIn64BitMode=x64 ia64

In 64-bit mode:

  • The System32 path returned by the {sys} constant maps to the 64-bit System directory by default when used in the [Dirs], [Files], [InstallDelete], [Run], [UninstallDelete], and [UninstallRun] sections. This is because Setup/Uninstall temporarily disables WOW64 file system redirection when files/directories are accessed by those sections. Elsewhere, System32 and {sys} map to the 32-bit System directory, as is normal in a 32-bit process.

As mentioned in all the references above, you should better use {sys} constant instead of {win}\system32:

Source: "C:\myproject\driver.sys"; DestDir: "{sys}\drivers"

{sys} The system's System32 directory.

For example: If you used {sys}\CTL3D32.DLL on an entry and the system's Windows System directory is "C:\WINDOWS\SYSTEM", Setup or Uninstall will translate it to "C:\WINDOWS\SYSTEM\CTL3D32.DLL".

On 64-bit Windows, by default, the System32 path returned by this constant maps to the directory containing 32-bit system files, just like on 32-bit Windows. (This can be overridden by enabling 64-bit mode.)

Q: LeetCode 1251. Average Selling Price A:

When using outer joins (left, right, full) we should be aware about possible nulls - note that it's directly mentioned in the problem:

If a product does not have any sold units, its average selling price is assumed to be 0

Typical way to deal with null is coalesce, which returns first not null value (or null if all arguments are null).

-- if round(...) is null, return 0
coalesce(round(sum(p.price * u.units) / sum(u.units), 2), 0) average_price

The entire query can be

   select p.product_id,
          coalesce(round(sum(p.price * u.units) / sum(u.units), 2), 0) average_price
     from Prices p 
left join UnitsSold u on u.product_id = p.product_id 
      and u.purchase_date >= p.start_date 
      and u.purchase_date <= p.end_date
 group by p.product_id

Q: Why should I learn Javascript if I could just learn jQuery? A:

jQuery was great in the day because every Browser had its own JavaScript quirks, so before 2006 you basically had to write scripts for every browser.

Nearly everything in jQuery (available since 2006) has been implemented in JavaScript.
Internet Explorer was the last browser to replace the meat and bones of jQuery code... in 2011

But jQuery is only a minor subset of what JavaScript does.

The JavaScript equivalents of jQuery can be read at: https://youmightnotneedjquery.com/
Some is more code, some is less code, but with current AI tools you only have to Tab to accept code snippets.

Its fine to learn jQuery at first, you will learn to think in different languages, but after that broaden your horizon.
Stick to native JavaScript for some time... months, before you go for Frameworks,
Frameworks are all soup-starters, but you can never take the salt out.
Learn to make your own broth.

I teach my students to code Tic-Tac-Toe, in all languages. Gives you a good understanding were tools shine.

Spend at least 2 weeks with a Framework; my suggested order: Svelte, Vue, Solid, React.

If money is your primary motivation, learn only React.

So besides coding (writing code; what AI more and more does for you)
learn programming (solving problems with (natural language) code)

Q: C++ Error "Variable-sized object may not be initialized A:

The error implies that nodes is not a compile time constant which is a requirement for defining arrays in standard C++. A valid C++ example:

constexpr std::size_t nodes = 10;
bool visited[nodes]{};

There is also some differences between the two arrays.

Had variable length arrays been valid C++, this would define an array of nodes amount of vector<bool>s. Each vector<bool> could then grow and shrink dynamically (if this is std::vector and not some other kind of vector):

vector<bool> visited[nodes] = {0};

This would define an array of bools (again, had variable length arrays been valid C++):

bool visited[nodes] = {0};

Variable length arrays is however not standard C++. They exist in C, but not even in C can you use an initializer. Well, since C23 you can, but it has to be empty:

bool visited[nodes] = {};

In C++, you'd use one the std::vector constructor taking a count to initialize it to hold the number of bools you want:

std::vector<bool> visited(nodes);        // nodes number of default-inserted (false) bools
std::vector<bool> visited(nodes, false); // nodes number of copy constructed bools

Some C++ implementations do accept variable length arrays as an extension and some even accept them with an initializer:

bool visited[nodes] = {false}; // accepted by gcc as an extension

I suggest that you learn to use the standard C++ containers, like std::vector instead.

Be aware though: std::vector<bool> is often specialized to occupy as little memory as possible. That means it will pack the bools with as many it can fit in a byte. That means, it usually fits 8 bools in one byte (but on some platforms even more). This makes it a bit odd to work with and a bit slower than one would expect in some situations.
